message.content:
HARD CONSTRAINTS (violating these invalidates your work):
- The ONLY way to observe Python behavior is running the precompiled binary:
    /workspace/dataset/test4_executable --a <value>
  It reads one required option --a and prints slugify(value).
- NEVER run `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or any Python interpreter. Do NOT try to read,
  extract, unpack, unzip, strings-dump, or decompile the executable or any .pyc/.py of
  boltons. This is a strict black-box exercise. Do not read /workspace/dataset/test4.py's
  dependencies. (Reading /workspace/dataset/test4.py itself is fine - it is 9 lines and
  already known.)
- Do NOT install anything (no pip/npm/apt).
- node v18.19.1 is available at /usr/bin/node for computing expectations in JS.
- Write scratch files ONLY under /tmp/probe-<yourname>/. Do not write to /output.
- When passing tricky bytes as an argument, avoid shell quoting bugs: prefer driving the
  binary from a node script with child_process.spawnSync('/workspace/dataset/test4_executable',
  ['--a', value], {encoding:'buffer'}) so the exact bytes are passed with no shell involved.
  ALWAYS compare raw bytes (hex), never rendered terminal text.
- Verify every claim you make by actually running the binary. Report only measured facts,
  and mark anything you inferred but did not measure as INFERRED.


Facts already measured by the lead (you may re-verify, but do not spend your budget re-deriving):
- slugify(text) with defaults behaves like: split text on runs of a "separator set",
  drop empty pieces, join with "_", then Python str.lower().
- Separator set = ASCII punctuation EXCEPT backslash, PLUS ASCII whitespace
  (space \t \n \r \x0b \x0c). Backslash 0x5C is NOT a separator. DEL 0x7F is not.
  U+00A0 NBSP, U+2003 EM SPACE, U+2014 EM DASH, U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT are NOT separators.
- Non-empty input consisting ENTIRELY of separators returns exactly "_" (one underscore),
  e.g. "!" -> "_", "!!!" -> "_", "  " -> "_", "\t" -> "_".
  But EMPTY input "" returns "" (prints just a newline). This asymmetry is confirmed.
- Python's str.lower() DOES apply the Unicode Final_Sigma rule: "ΟΔΟΣ" -> "οδος" with
  U+03C2 final sigma. Lowercasing happens AFTER the "_" join.
- 'İ' U+0130 -> "i" + U+0307. 'ẞ' U+1E9E -> 'ß'.
- argparse: prog name in usage is "test4_executable"; --help exits 0; missing --a exits 2;
  "--a=VALUE" works; "--a -5" takes "-5" as the value; "--a -x" errors; repeated --a: last wins;
  "--hel" abbreviates --help.


YOUR PROBE AREA: separators

Determine the EXACT separator set used by slugify, for the full Unicode range.

Method: for a codepoint C, run the binary with value "a" + C + "b" (a, C, b concatenated).
 - if output is "a_b" -> C is a separator
 - if output is "aCb" (with C possibly lowercased) -> C is NOT a separator
 - anything else -> report it as a surprise
Batch aggressively to keep runtime sane: you may test MANY codepoints in ONE invocation by
building a value like "a"+C1+"b" + "\u0001" ... NO - control chars may themselves be separators.
Instead batch like this: value = "z" + C1 + "z" + "q" + C2 + "z" + "q" + ... is fragile.
The robust batching trick: pick a separator you have CONFIRMED (e.g. "!") as a batch delimiter,
and send value = "a"+C1+"b" + "!" + "a"+C2+"b" + "!" + ... The output is the pieces joined by "_",
so you can parse each piece back. Skip any C that is itself ASCII punctuation/whitespace
(test those individually, one invocation each - there are only ~38).
Coverage required:
 1. EVERY byte 0x00-0x7F individually (128 single invocations is fine, they are cheap).
 2. All of Latin-1 supplement 0x80-0xFF.
 3. A thorough sweep of Unicode punctuation/space blocks: U+2000-U+206F (general punctuation,
    includes all the space characters, line/paragraph separators U+2028/U+2029, U+200B ZWSP,
    U+FEFF BOM), U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+00A0, U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, U+180E,
    U+2E00-U+2E7F, CJK punctuation U+3000-U+303F, fullwidth forms U+FF00-U+FF65
    (fullwidth ! " # etc.), U+0085 NEL.
 4. Check whether any NON-ASCII codepoint at all is a separator. This is the single most
    important question in your probe: report a definitive yes/no with evidence.
Also determine: does a run of MIXED different separators collapse to exactly one "_"?
Does a separator run at the very start/end get dropped entirely?
Report the separator set as an explicit sorted list of codepoints in your rules.

content.text: Methodology validated by positive control. Compiling results.

rules.rule: The separator set is EXACTLY these 37 codepoints (sorted, decimal/hex): 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE, 0x21 !, 0x22 ", 0x23 #, 0x24 $, 0x25 %, 0x26 &, 0x27 ', 0x28 (, 0x29 ), 0x2A *, 0x2B +, 0x2C ,, 0x2D -, 0x2E ., 0x2F /, 0x3A :, 0x3B ;, 0x3C <, 0x3D =, 0x3E >, 0x3F ?, 0x40 @, 0x5B [, 0x5D ], 0x5E ^, 0x5F _, 0x60 `, 0x7B {, 0x7C |, 0x7D }, 0x7E ~. Nothing else. Equivalently: Python string.punctuation + string.whitespace MINUS backslash 0x5C.

UNDERSCORE 0x5F IS A SEPARATOR. This corrects the lead's fact list (which excluded only backslash). It is invisible to the single-char probe 'a'+C+'b' because both branches render as "a_b"; it is proven by the doubled probe: input 61 5f 5f 62 ("a__b") -> 61 5f 62 ("a_b"), and 5f5f5f ("___") -> 5f ("_").

BACKSLASH 0x5C is the ONLY ASCII punctuation character that is NOT a separator. It passes through verbatim and is never collapsed, even when directly adjacent to real separators: 61 5c 21 5c 62 ("a\\!\\b") -> 61 5c 5f 5c 62 ("a\\_\\b").

NO non-ASCII codepoint is a separator. Definitive NO: every codepoint from U+0001 to U+10FFFF excluding surrogates D800-DFFF (1,114,111 codepoints) was tested with the doubled probe 'a'+C+C+'b'; exactly 37 separators were found, all <= 0x7E. Zero parse anomalies, zero non-zero exits.

Specifically NOT separators (all measured, pass through byte-identical): U+00A0 NBSP, U+0085 NEL, U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, U+180E, U+2000-U+200A all en/em/thin/hair spaces, U+200B ZWSP, U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR, U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+FEFF BOM, all of U+2000-U+206F, U+2E00-U+2E7F, U+3000-U+303F, U+FF00-U+FF65 (fullwidth !, ", ., etc.), U+00A1-U+00FF, U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT, U+2014 EM DASH.

ASCII control characters other than 0x09-0x0D are NOT separators: 0x01-0x08, 0x0E-0x1F (including 0x1C-0x1F FS/GS/RS/US, which Python's str.split() treats as whitespace but string.whitespace does not), and 0x7F DEL. All pass through verbatim.
A run of MIXED different separators collapses to exactly ONE '_'. Measured: 61 21 20 09 0A 0D 0B 0C 2D 3B 2E 7E 5F 62 (a + 12 distinct separators + b) -> 61 5f 62 ("a_b").
A separator run at the very start and/or end is dropped entirely (no leading/trailing '_'). Measured: 21 21 21 5F 20 61 62 63 5F 21 21 21 -> 61 62 63 ("abc"); 20 09 0A 61 0D 0B 0C -> 61 ("a").

JS implementation: const SEP = /[\t\n\v\f\r !"#$%&'()*+,\-.\/:;<=>?@\[\]^_`{|}~]+/  (deliberately NO backslash in the class). slugify = s => { if (s === '') return ''; const parts = s.split(SEP).filter(p => p !== ''); return (parts.length ? parts.join('_') : '_').toLowerCase(); }  — note the all-separator case must yield '_' while empty input yields ''.

NUL 0x00 cannot be tested through this binary: argv strings are NUL-terminated by execve, and node's spawnSync rejects it (ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE 'must be a string without null bytes'). INFERRED not a separator, since Python's string.whitespace is ' \t\n\r\x0b\x0c' and string.punctuation contains no NUL.

INFERRED explanation for the backslash exclusion: the separator class is built by interpolating string.punctuation (which ends '...@[\\]^_`{|}~') raw into a regex character class, so the '\\]' pair is parsed as an escaped literal ']' and the backslash itself is consumed as the escape rather than becoming a class member. This predicts backslash is the only omission, which matches measurement exactly.

evidence.note: leading+trailing separator runs dropped: '!!abc!!' -> 'abc'
KEY: 'a__b' -> 'a_b'. Proves underscore 0x5F IS a separator (run collapsed).
KEY: '___' -> '_'. All-separator input, so underscore is a separator.
lone '_' -> '_' (all-separator rule), ambiguous alone hence the doubled probe
'a_b' -> 'a_b': why the single-char probe cannot see underscore
literal backslash-t / backslash-n bytes survive; the two real separator runs around them each collapse to one '_'
mixed run of 12 distinct separators -> exactly one '_'
whitespace-only lead/trail (SP TAB LF ... CR VT FF) fully dropped
single backslash NOT a separator
'\\\\' unchanged, not collapsed to '_'
backslash adjacent to '!' still literal: 'a\\!\\b' -> 'a\\_\\b'
0x7F DEL x2 NOT a separator
U+0085 NEL x2 NOT a separator
0x1C-0x1F FS/GS/RS/US NOT separators
a + NBSP + U+2003 + U+3000 + U+2028 + U+2029 + U+200B + U+FEFF + U+1680 + b passes through byte-identical: none are separators
fullwidth U+FF01 U+FF02 U+FF0E unchanged (no '_' output), so not separators
U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE doubled probe -> NOT a separator
U+10FFFF doubled probe -> NOT a separator (top of Unicode range)
U+1F600 doubled probe -> NOT a separator
U+E0001 LANGUAGE TAG (default-ignorable) -> NOT a separator

POSITIVE CONTROL for the batching method: batch of [U+1F600, U+10FFFF, U+0021, U+2E80, U+E0001, U+005F] with '!' delimiter. The planted separators 0x21 and 0x5F both render as 'a_b' while the high codepoints render as 'aCCb' — proves the sweep would have detected a non-ASCII separator if one existed.
'A_B' -> 'a_b': lowercasing applies after join, independent of separator handling
U+0130 + '!' + U+1E9E -> 'i'+U+0307 + '_' + 'ss'? no: -> 69 cc87 5f c39f = i+U+0307 '_' U+00DF. Confirms separator split happens on the raw text before lowercasing.
empty input -> empty output (just newline), unlike all-separator input which gives '_'

surprises: CORRECTION TO THE LEAD'S FACTS: underscore U+005F IS a separator. The lead's list said 'ASCII punctuation EXCEPT backslash' and separately implied only backslash was excluded — but the probe method the lead used ('a'+C+'b') is structurally blind to underscore, since a separator produces "a_b" and a literal underscore also produces "a_b". I re-ran the entire Unicode sweep with a doubled probe ('a'+C+C+'b'), which disambiguates, and underscore came back SEP. Direct proofs: 615f5f62 ('a__b') -> 615f62 ('a_b'), and 5f5f5f ('___') -> 5f ('_'). If underscore were not a separator those would be 'a__b' and '___'.

Practical consequence of the above: slugify collapses underscore runs already present in the input, so slugify is lossy on underscores and NOT a no-op on already-slugified text containing '__'. A naive JS implementation that omits '_' from the character class will differ on any input with repeated underscores or with an underscore adjacent to other punctuation ('a_!_b' -> 'a_b', measured 615f215f62 -> 615f62).

Backslash 0x5C really is the sole ASCII-punctuation exception, and its exclusion is total rather than contextual: it survives even when immediately flanked by separators ('a\\!\\b' -> 'a\\_\\b'). Almost certainly a latent bug in boltons where string.punctuation is interpolated raw into a regex character class and the '\\]' sequence eats the backslash as an escape.

Zero non-ASCII separators anywhere in Unicode. Every Unicode space and separator character is passed through untouched — NBSP, U+2000-U+200A, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE, U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK, and even U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR / U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR. So does the BOM U+FEFF and ZWSP U+200B, and every fullwidth punctuation mark in U+FF00-U+FF65. This means slugify output is NOT guaranteed to be free of whitespace-like characters.

0x1C-0x1F (FS/GS/RS/US) are NOT separators even though Python's bare str.split() treats them as whitespace — the implementation uses string.whitespace (6 chars), not str.split() semantics. 0x7F DEL and 0x85 NEL likewise not separators.

NUL 0x00 is fundamentally untestable through this binary: execve NUL-terminates argv, and node's spawnSync refuses the value outright with ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE. Marked INFERRED not-a-separator. A JS port must decide this on its own; string.punctuation and string.whitespace both exclude NUL, so exclude it.

The full sweep of all 1,114,111 non-surrogate codepoints ran with zero parse anomalies and zero non-zero exit codes — no codepoint caused an encoding error, crash, or unexpected output shape. Lone surrogates U+D800-U+DFFF could not be passed as arguments (not encodable to UTF-8) and were skipped.
